title: What They Remembered
subtitle: Past-Life Sessions, Honestly Told
thesis: A regression session is testimony: an accurate record of what a person said and felt in a chair, and not a record of the world outside it. This book reports eight sessions in full, checks every claim inside them that can be checked, says plainly what came back, and argues that what the work does for a person is worth taking seriously whether or not the past life is.
back_cover:
She described the staircase before I asked about the house.

I have sat with people in that chair for years, and I can tell you exactly what they say when they get there. This book reports eight sessions in full: the words, the pauses, the crying, the things that came out in a voice the person does not use. Where a session touched something that can be looked up — a name, a date, a place, an object — I looked it up, and I tell you what came back, including the times it came back empty.

What I will not do is dress a session up as proof. A regression is testimony, not history, and the difference is the whole book. You will finish it knowing what happens minute by minute in a session, what a practitioner should refuse to promise you, how to prepare for your own, and how to read every other account on this shelf without either swallowing it whole or throwing it out.

chapters.title: A Note on How This Book Reports Things
chapters.summary: Before any session is told, the reader is given the ground rules: where the accounts come from, what has been changed to protect the people in them, what is reported as testimony and what has been checked against the record. Short, plain and binding on every page that follows.
beats: Who I am, how long I have done this, and what I am not
The rule this book keeps: what was said in the chair, and what stands up outside it, reported separately
What has been altered — names, jobs, towns — and the one category of detail that never is
What you will and will not find here, said plainly enough to put the book down now

chapters.title: The Question Everyone Asks Me First
chapters.summary: Opens with the question every new client and every sceptic asks — do you believe it's real? — and gives the answer that shapes the entire book: I can tell you what was said, and I can tell you what checks out, and those are two different reports. Sets the terms of the deal between writer and reader before a single session is told.
beats: The question asked in the intake chair and the question asked at dinner parties: same words, different weight
Why 'do you believe it' is the wrong question to hand a practitioner, and what I answer instead
The two reports this book will keep separate on every page: what was said, what stands up
What I am asking of the reader in exchange: stay for the sessions even where the record comes back empty

chapters.title: Testimony and History Are Not the Same Word
chapters.summary: Makes the book's central distinction concrete and usable rather than philosophical: testimony is a true account of what a person experienced, history is a claim about the world, and a session produces the first while readers are routinely sold the second. Gives the reader the distinction as a tool they will use in every chapter that follows.
beats: A courtroom keeps the two apart with a single question: are you telling us what you saw, or what happened?
Everything said in a session is real testimony even when nothing in it is history
The three places the slide from one to the other happens: the transcript, the retelling, the book cover
Why keeping them apart costs a writer nothing and buys the reader everything

chapters.title: The Same Session, Told Twice
chapters.summary: Takes one short session and reports it two ways on facing pages: once as testimony, once the way this shelf usually tells it. Nothing is added between the two versions and nothing is invented — only the framing changes — and the reader sees exactly how much a reader is asked to accept when the framing shifts.
beats: Version one: what she said, what she felt, where she stopped, in her own words and mine
Version two: the same forty minutes written as a recovered life, with every verb hardened
Line by line: the seven places version two makes a claim version one never made
Why version two sells better in the first ten pages and worse in the last ten

chapters.title: Six Words I Refuse to Use, and What I Say Instead
chapters.summary: The vocabulary of honesty, given as a working list: six words common in this field that smuggle in a claim, and the plainer phrases I use in their place with clients and in this book. Shows that the discipline is not a matter of disclaimers but of ordinary word choice, sentence by sentence.
beats: 'Remembered', 'recalled', 'returned to', 'proved', 'confirmed', 'verified' — what each one quietly asserts
The replacements I actually say out loud in the room, and how clients react to them
Why the hedge belongs in the sentence and not in a note at the back of the book
A short passage rewritten with the six words removed, to show what survives

chapters.title: What Gets Written Down, and What Gets Lost
chapters.summary: How the record in this book was made: the recording, my notes, the consent, and the changes I make to protect the people in the chair. States plainly that names and identifying details are altered and that some accounts combine sessions, so the reader knows the provenance of every word before the first session begins.
beats: The recorder, the notebook, and the gap between what is captured and what is remembered by me
Consent, anonymity, and the details I change — and the rule that no changed detail is ever a checkable one
Why I mark composites as composites instead of letting the reader assume
What is lost when speech becomes a transcript: pace, silence, the breath before an answer

chapters.title: Before Anyone Closes Their Eyes
chapters.summary: The hour before the session — the intake conversation — which decides more about what happens than the induction does. Shows what I ask, what I listen for, what I refuse to take on, and how a client's expectations get named out loud before they can be mistaken for content.
beats: The four questions I ask everyone, and why the answer to the second one changes the session
Naming the expectation: what the client is hoping to find, said aloud so it can be told apart from what arrives
Who I turn away, and the two reasons I give them
Setting the terms: what I will not do, agreed before the chair reclines

chapters.title: The Induction, Minute by Minute
chapters.summary: A complete walk through the induction for a reader who has never had a session: what is said, what the body does, how long each stage takes, what it feels like from the inside. Demystifies the part of the work that is usually described in either clinical or mystical language and almost never in plain minutes.
beats: Minutes nought to five: the chair, the breathing, the script, the reason the script is boring on purpose
Minutes five to fifteen: deepening, and the signs I watch for that tell me it is working
What 'under' actually means — awake, aware, able to stop, and why clients are surprised by that
The people it does not work on, and how quickly I can tell

chapters.title: The Questions I Ask, and the Ones I Have Learned Not To
chapters.summary: The most consequential craft in this work: a question can hand a client the answer without either of them noticing. Sets out the open questions I use, the leading ones I have stripped from my practice, and what happened in the sessions that taught me the difference.
beats: 'What are you aware of?' against 'What century is it?' — the same silence, two different sessions
The leading question I used for two years before I heard myself on a recording
Why I never supply a noun the client has not already used
How a reader can spot a leading question in any transcript, including the ones in this book

chapters.title: Their Words, Not Mine
chapters.summary: What a session actually sounds like on the recording, as opposed to how it reads when it has been tidied. Presents unedited stretches of speech — fragmentary, repetitive, present tense, oddly specific about small things — so the reader learns the texture of genuine session talk and can hear when an account has been smoothed.
beats: A four-minute stretch transcribed exactly, hesitations and all
Why the details that arrive are small and domestic rather than grand and datable
The present tense, the shifting pronouns, and the voice that is not quite theirs
What tidying a transcript removes, and why I have stopped doing it

chapters.title: Coming Back: the Last Ten Minutes Nobody Writes About
chapters.summary: The return is the part of the session that books skip and practitioners cannot afford to, because it determines what the client walks out carrying. Covers the count up, the re-orientation, the first thing people say, and the care that belongs to the hour after rather than the hour during.
beats: How I bring someone back, and why I never do it quickly
The first sentence out of a client's mouth, and what I have learned from collecting them
Grogginess, tears, hunger, elation: the ordinary physical aftermath, described honestly
What I say before they drive home, and the note I send two days later

chapters.title: What I Will Not Do in That Room
chapters.summary: The refusals that define a serious practice: no diagnosis, no prophecy, no guarantees, no reading of a person who is not present. Explains the reasoning behind each one and what I say when a client pushes, which they sometimes do and sometimes for heartbreaking reasons.
beats: No diagnosis: what a client brings that belongs to a doctor, and how I hand it back
No prophecy: the request I get most often and refuse most firmly
No third parties: why I will not put an absent person in the chair by proxy
No guarantees: the sentence I say in the intake and repeat in the invoice

chapters.title: The Woman Who Counted Stairs
chapters.summary: The first full session in the book, reported end to end: a client who arrived about something else entirely and spent forty minutes describing a staircase she counted every time she climbed it. Includes what was said, what she felt, what changed for her, and the short note on what in it could be checked.
beats: What she came for, and why it had nothing to do with stairs
The session in her words: the count, the cold, the door she would not open
What she reported in the weeks after, in her own account rather than my summary
The check: one detail that could be looked up, what I found, and what I did not conclude from it

chapters.title: The Man Who Could Not Swim
chapters.summary: A session with a client whose fear of open water had survived three courses of ordinary treatment, and what arrived when he stopped trying to explain it. The chapter is as interested in the fear as in the content, because the fear is the part that can be observed before and after.
beats: Forty years of avoiding water, described by the person avoiding it
What he said in the chair, including the two minutes he could not speak
The swimming lesson he booked eleven weeks later, and what he says about it now
The check: nothing in this session was checkable, and why that is worth stating plainly

chapters.title: A Kitchen, a Window, and a Name She Could Not Pronounce
chapters.summary: A session unusually rich in specifics — a room described in detail, a name repeated a dozen times — which is exactly the kind of account that gets presented elsewhere as evidence. Reports it in full and then reports the search honestly: the record has nothing to say about it either way.
beats: The room she described, item by item, including the two things she got wrong about her own house
The name, phonetically transcribed, and her frustration at not being able to hold it
What I searched, where I searched it, and how long I spent
Coming back empty: what that does and does not tell us, and why the session still stands as testimony

chapters.title: The Session That Checked Out, and Why I Still Won't Call It Proof
chapters.summary: The one session in this book where a specific detail matched something findable in the record — and the follow-up conversation that showed where the client had almost certainly met that detail before, at eight years old, on a school trip. The most honest chapter in the book and the one readers will argue with.
beats: The detail, stated exactly as she stated it, before I knew what it was
Finding the match, and the forty minutes when I thought I had something
The school trip, the leaflet, and the ordinary explanation that arrived a month later
What a hit is actually worth once you count how many chances a session gets to produce one

chapters.title: The Soldier Who Would Not Give a Date
chapters.summary: A session with a client who described a war in vivid sensory detail and, asked directly, could not or would not say when or where. Uses the refusal as a way into a pattern that is common in this work and almost never reported, because it makes for a less satisfying story.
beats: The mud, the weight of the pack, the sound he kept coming back to
Three attempts to establish a when, and three answers that went nowhere
Why I stopped pressing, and what pressing would have produced
The check: no date, no place, nothing to look up — and the reason that is more common than the alternative

chapters.title: Two Sisters, One Room, Two Different Lives
chapters.summary: Two clients who booked together, sat in the same chair a fortnight apart, and produced accounts with almost nothing in common. Reports both, notes the two small places they touched, and uses the pair to show how much a session is shaped by the person rather than the procedure.
beats: The older sister's session, and the expectation she arrived carrying
The younger sister's session, which went somewhere neither of them predicted
The two overlaps, described precisely, and the arithmetic of how surprising they really are
What they said to each other afterwards, and why I let them compare notes despite my usual rule

chapters.title: The Session I Stopped
chapters.summary: An account of a session I ended early, why I ended it, and what I did next — the chapter that exists because duty of care is not a disclaimer but a decision made in real time. Names the signals I watch for and the referral I made afterwards.
beats: What I saw in the first fifteen minutes that made me change plan
How you end a session safely when it is not going where it should
The conversation afterwards, and the referral he did and did not take up
The three signals that now stop a session in my practice, written out for other practitioners

chapters.title: What a Session Sounds Like When Nothing Happens
chapters.summary: The last of the eight full sessions is the one that produced nothing: no scenes, no voice, no lifetime, an hour of a man lying quietly and reporting the colour behind his eyelids. It is in the book because leaving it out is how this shelf ends up misrepresenting the work.
beats: An hour transcribed almost in full, because there is little to transcribe
What I tried, in order, and why I stopped trying
What he said about the session afterwards, which was not what I expected
How often this happens in my practice, and why nobody puts it in a book

chapters.title: Eight Sessions, One Threshold: What Repeats and What Never Does
chapters.summary: Steps back from the eight accounts and reports the patterns across them as patterns: thresholds, staircases, water, the reluctance to give numbers, the sensory details that arrive first. States clearly that a recurring pattern is a fact about sessions, not evidence about lives.
beats: What repeats in these eight and across the wider run of my practice: the threshold, the small domestic object, the weather
What almost never arrives unprompted: dates, surnames, place names, anything a reader could check
Why that asymmetry is the single most interesting finding in this book
Three readings of the pattern, including two that do not require a past life, presented without picking one

chapters.title: Why Almost Nobody Is a Nobody
chapters.summary: Deals with the famous-lifetime problem directly and without mockery: why prominent identities surface far more often than population arithmetic allows, what I say when one arrives in my room, and how to hold the session respectfully while declining the claim.
beats: The arithmetic, done simply: how many people ever lived, and how many of them anyone has heard of
What arrives in my room, honestly counted across the sessions I have run
What I do when a famous name surfaces — which is not to contradict the client mid-session
The conversation afterwards, and why it is possible to honour the experience and decline the identification

chapters.title: Dates, Names, and the Records That Are Supposed to Settle Them
chapters.summary: What actually happens when you try to check a session against the documentary record: which records exist, how patchy they are, what a match is worth and what an absence does not settle. The chapter that keeps the reader from over-reading both a hit and a miss.
beats: The four kinds of record a session claim usually has to be checked against, and how complete each one is
Why an absence of record is weak evidence in both directions, with a worked example
What counts as a match, and the three ways a loose match gets reported as a tight one
The check I now run before any session detail goes into writing, step by step

chapters.title: Buried Objects, Buried Arguments
chapters.summary: The physical-evidence claim — the box under the floor, the ring in the wall, the thing that would settle it — and why it almost never survives contact with the actual world. Treats the wish behind the claim seriously while explaining why I no longer chase them.
beats: Three times a client told me where something was buried, and what I did about it
What it actually takes to dig somewhere: permission, ownership, cost, and the law
Why 'they found it exactly where she said' stories collapse when you ask for the chain of custody
The honest version of this claim, which is smaller and more interesting than the dramatic one

chapters.title: The First Thing a Sceptical Reader Looks Up
chapters.summary: Written for the reader who has already been burned: a straight account of how one checkable error destroys the credibility of an entire book, why it is the first thing anyone verifies, and what an author owes a reader who is willing to check. Explains the standard this book has tried to hold itself to.
beats: The reader who checks one claim, finds it wrong, and stops believing the sessions too
Why the checkable details are always the weakest part of an account and always the most quoted
The standard I set for this book, stated as a rule anyone can test against these pages
What to do when you find an error in a book you otherwise valued, including this one

chapters.title: Where the Material Comes From When It Isn't a Past Life
chapters.summary: Lays out the ordinary explanations — forgotten sources, suggestion, the mind's talent for narrative — fully and fairly, because a reader who has not met them cannot evaluate anything in this book. Written without condescension: these explanations account for a great deal and are not an insult to anyone's experience.
beats: Forgotten sources: the documentary at eleven, the book on a grandparent's shelf, the film half-watched
Suggestion, and how little of it is needed — demonstrated with a question from chapter eight
The narrative instinct: why the mind produces a coherent story rather than noise
What these explanations do not account for, stated as carefully as what they do

chapters.title: Reading the Rest of the Shelf
chapters.summary: Hands the reader a working filter for every other account of this work they will encounter, without naming or disparaging any of it. Six questions to ask of any regression book, article or video, each one answerable from the text itself in under a minute.
beats: Question one: does the account separate what was said from what is being claimed?
Questions two to four: sourcing, checkability, and what the writer says about failures
Questions five and six: what is promised, and who is not in the room
Applying all six to this book, out loud, including where it comes off worst

chapters.title: The Grief That Moved, and the Claim I Am Making About It
chapters.summary: The book's positive argument, stated precisely: what changes for people after this work is observable, reportable and worth something, and it is a claim about lives afterwards rather than lives before. Distinguishes it carefully from a promise, which this book does not make.
beats: Three clients' accounts of what was different at three months, in their words
What I am claiming: a change reported by the person, not an outcome I delivered
What I am not claiming: cure, treatment, or a result anyone can expect
Why a claim this modest is still the strongest one this field can honestly make

chapters.title: Recurring Dreams, Old Fears, and the Weeks After a Session
chapters.summary: What people bring to the chair and what tends to shift — dreams, fears, an unexplained pull towards a place — and, practically, what to do with the material in the fortnight after a session when it is still moving. The most useful chapter for a reader who has just had one.
beats: The three things people most often arrive with, and what they tend to say afterwards
The fortnight after: writing it down, sitting with it, and the mistake of deciding what it means too early
When to book a second session and when a second session is the wrong idea
When what has surfaced belongs with a therapist instead, and how to tell

chapters.title: How to Tell a Serious Practitioner From a Performer
chapters.summary: A buyer's chapter: the questions to ask before booking, the answers that should reassure you, and the ones that should end the conversation. Written from inside the profession, including the practices I think are indefensible and why.
beats: Seven questions to ask on the phone, with the answers a serious practitioner gives
The four answers that should end the call, including the one that sounds most impressive
Price, length, recording, consent: what is normal and what is a warning
What a good practitioner refuses to promise you, and why the refusal is the reassurance

chapters.title: Your First Session: What to Bring, What to Ask, What Nobody Can Promise
chapters.summary: The practical close: how to prepare for a first session, what to carry into the room, what to establish before you close your eyes, and what a reasonable expectation looks like. Ends the book where it began, with testimony rather than promises.
beats: The week before: sleep, food, and the one thing not to do the night before
What to bring: a question rather than a hypothesis, and why the distinction matters
What to establish before the chair reclines, in the practitioner's hearing
What a reasonable expectation looks like, and the sentence to be suspicious of

chapters.title: What I Think, for What It Is Worth
chapters.summary: Having kept my own opinion out of thirty chapters, I give it here, clearly marked as an opinion and not as a finding. Closes the book by repeating the only claim it has actually made and leaving the larger question where it belongs, with the reader.
beats: The one claim this book has made, restated in a single sentence
What I personally think happens in that chair, offered as a belief and labelled as one
Why I have kept it to the last four pages instead of the first
What I would want a reader to carry out of here, whichever way they end up
